text: Dame Elizabeth Anne Loosemore Esteve-Coll DBE FRSA (née Kingdon; 14 October 1938 – 16 September 2024) was a British academic, museum director, and librarian. She was born in Ripon, West Riding of Yorkshire, the daughter of Percy Kingdon, a bank clerk, and his wife Nora Rose. She attended Darlington High School and studied English and Spanish at Trinity College, Dublin, followed by Art History at Birkbeck College (now Birkbeck, University of London).[2][3] From 1977 to 1982, she served as head of learning resources at Kingston Polytechnic (now Kingston University London).[4] In 1982, she became the first female director of the University of Surrey Library.[4][5] In 1985, she was appointed Keeper of the National Art Library at the Victoria and Albert Museum, where she initiated changes to increase accessibility for a broader audience.[7] In 1987, she became the UK's first woman director of a national arts collection, succeeding Sir Roy Strong, and held the position until her resignation in 1994, midway through her second term, to become Vice-Chancellor of the University of East Anglia.[8][9] Alan Borg succeeded her as director, taking office on 1 October 1995.[8] She served as Vice-Chancellor of the University of East Anglia from 1995 to 1997 but stepped down after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, stating: "It is with real sadness and disappointment that I must acknowledge that I am not able to lead the university into the 21st century."[11][12] She served as Chancellor of the University of Lincoln for seven years and was a Trustee of the Sainsbury Institute for the Study of Japanese Arts and Cultures since its foundation in January 1999.[13][14] At the age of 21, she married José Esteve-Coll, a Spanish refugee sea captain who was 30 years her senior; he died in 1980.[15] She was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in the Queen's Birthday Honours list in 1995. In November 2005, she received the Order of the Rising Sun, Gold Rays with Neck Ribbon (3rd class) for her "outstanding contribution to the promotion of Japanese culture and studies to British people".[16] In November 2008, she was awarded an honorary doctorate of arts and named Chancellor Emerita by the University of Lincoln during a farewell ceremony at Lincoln Cathedral.[17][18] She died on 16 September 2024, at the age of 85.[15]
